newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish voters approve controversial constitution.
newsitem.headline: Polish voters approve controversial constitution.

text.p: Poles voted in a referendum on Sunday to adopt a new constitution backed by the ruling ex-communists and bitterly opposed by the rightist opposition grouped around the Solidarity union, an exit poll showed.

A poll by the Pracownia Badan Spolecznych (PBS) showed that 56.8 percent had voted for the new constitution and 43.2 were against in a turnout of 39.8 percent of Poland's 28 million voters, public television reported.
Final official results will not be available until Monday or Tuesday. But a PBS representative said previous such polls had never differed by more than one percent from official results.

The constitution, designed to enshrine Poland's democratic transformation since the 1989 fall of communism, was drafted by the ruling Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) and its Peasant allies with two opposition parties in parliament.

Those favouring a "yes" vote hailed the verdict but regretted the low turnout -- even though there was no minimum vote required to confirm the constitution, which was passed by parliament on April 2 and will take effect in just over three months.
President Aleksander Kwasniewski, a former communist, said he had hoped for a higher participation but praised the outcome.
"This constitution gives us a greater feeling of normality and stability," he said.

Solidarity and allied parties grouped in an alliance which aims to supplant the ex-communists in elections due in September had argued that it failed to reflect Poland's Christian traditions and safeguard national sovereignty.
The right put a brave face on the setback and senior union official Jacek Rybicki homed in on the low turnout, saying it proved a lack of clear support for the contested document.

"The most significant thing is that as many as 17 million Poles stayed at home...We will have to correct the disputed points (of this constitution) in the future parliament," Rybicki told public television.

The Solidarity Election Action (AWS), under-represented in parliament but rivalling the ex-communists for top place in pre-election polls with around 25 percent each, was angry that the referendum was pushed through so soon before elections that could change parliament's line-up.
Even before the vote, the right had said it would not regard a "yes" vote for the constitution as presaging defeat in the parliamentary elections.
A "no" verdict would have left Poland with remains of its discredited 1952 constitution, amended by 1992 interim laws, until some future parliament could agree on a new version.
The constitution broadly retains the current political system while weakening the presidency. It sets caps on the government's spending but obliges it to support employment and home building.

Solidarity, seeing Poland's history as bound up with the majority Roman Catholic faith, had wanted the charter to clearly invoke God, place religious values above man-made law and include a clause effectively banning abortion -- now legal in Poland.
The bishops, concerned over abortion, had voiced deep moral reservations about the current document.
Sunday's vote could also be seen as an indication of attitudes towards the Church before a May 31-June 10 visit by Polish Pope John Paul.
The right also said a section allowing Poland to surrender by treaty some functions to international organisations -- to ease entry into European structures -- limited sovereignty.
The constitution's authors rejected these arguments as false.
They said their version made room for people of all faiths or none and, for example, left open the possibility of changing the abortion law by a future majority in parliament.
